A jacket is decided by the shoulders and nothing else matters as much: the shoulder seam should end on your shoulder bone, and the padding should follow your own line rather than sit out past it, because a shoulder is the one thing a tailor cannot change much. Then check the chest - you should be able to slide a flat hand inside the buttoned jacket - the sleeve, which should end at the wrist bone and show about a centimetre of shirt cuff, and the seat, where the jacket should just cover it without flaring. Button the middle button only and sit down in it before you decide.

Hibernation is a way of getting through a season with no food: the animal's temperature, heart rate and breathing drop, and it lives off the fat it laid down in autumn. A bear's heart can slow from 40 beats a minute to 8, and a hedgehog turns almost cold to the touch. A bat or a hedgehog woken in winter has spent a lot of energy for nothing, so leave one be.

Do two or three sets of eight to twelve, and add a little each week - more reps, a slower lower, a heavier bag - because muscle only grows when the last rep is hard. Two sessions a week beats five that you stop after a fortnight.

Most adult dogs need 30 minutes to an hour a day, and a working breed rather more. A puppy is the other way round: about five minutes of walking for every month of age, twice a day, so a four-month-old gets two twenty-minute walks and no long hikes or stair runs until the growth plates close at a year. Flat-faced breeds and older dogs need less and overheat easily, so go by the dog rather than the breed chart. Running or cycling with a dog is the same rule at speed: wait until he is a year old, start with a mile and add a little each week, keep it on soft ground, and skip it on warm days, because a dog on hot tarmac is burnt pads and heat stroke.

Owning means noticing when it needs doing, not waiting to be asked, so agree a standard rather than a method ("the kitchen is clear by bedtime" can be checked; "do it properly" cannot). Revisit it once a month while the system beds in, and say thank you out loud when you notice something, because a split that nobody mentions still feels unfair.

Go at the time you would actually go, on a weekday evening if that is when you are free: a gym that is full at six is the one you stop using. Then check three things - the distance from home or work, because anything past fifteen minutes gets skipped, whether the classes you want are included in the price or cost extra, and the notice period on the contract, which is often a month and sometimes three. Universal Credit is claimed online at gov.uk in one form for everything, and you can ask for an advance of the first payment on the same call - it is repaid slowly from later payments, so ask for it rather than borrowing. Have your bank details, housing costs and childcare costs ready, because the first payment takes about five weeks and the advance is what covers that gap. Child Benefit is a separate form (CH2) and is worth backdating: claim within three months of the birth or you lose the money. Citizens Advice will check what else you qualify for, free.

They are not the same: baking soda is pure bicarbonate and needs an acid (buttermilk, yoghurt, lemon, treacle) to make things rise, while baking powder already has the acid in it. One way is easy and the other is not: in place of a teaspoon of soda use about three teaspoons of baking powder, and put the acid the recipe counted on in some other way or the tang is lost; in place of a teaspoon of baking powder use a quarter teaspoon of bicarbonate with a teaspoon of lemon juice or vinegar, and only in something that has the acid to meet.

A houseplant flops over for one of three reasons: it has grown tall and thin reaching for light, the pot has become top-heavy for its roots, or the roots have rotted in soggy compost and let go. Move it somewhere brighter, put a cane or a hoop in and tie the stems loosely, and check the drainage holes before you water again - a pot standing in a full saucer is the usual cause.

The phone is a radio with a small computer in it: it finds the nearest mast, tells the network it is there, and every call or page is passed from mast to mast as you move. The aerial on a mast covers a few hundred metres in town, which is why the same phone works in one room and not the next.

Fix the wake-up time first: the same hour every day, including after a bad night, and the rest tends to follow within a fortnight.
